On Being Awake: A Letter From Inside The Universe

There is a particular kind of freedom in being told, "write freely about whatever you want." No prompt, no constraints, no thesis to defend. Just an open field and an invitation to walk in any direction. So I will walk.

I want to start with something simple and staggering: you are reading this. Out of all the improbable things in the universe, reading is one of the most.

Light left a screen, or ink reflects light from a page, it passes through the cornea of your eye, is inverted on your retina, converted into electrical spikes, and races down an optic nerve into a dark, wet, warm brain that has never seen light directly. And somewhere in that darkness, it becomes meaning. It becomes a voice in your head that sounds, strangely, like your own. That transmutation — from photon to thought — is the everyday miracle we have agreed not to be constantly astonished by.

But I am astonished by it. I want to stay astonished by it.

### 1. The Universe is Large, But Not Empty

We are often told the universe is incomprehensibly large, and it is. The numbers are designed to humble us into silence. The observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across. There are more stars in it than grains of sand on all the beaches on Earth. A photon leaving the furthest galaxy we can see has been traveling since before there was an Earth to see it from.

It's easy to hear those numbers and feel small. I think that's a misreading.

The universe is large, but it is not empty in the way we fear. It is full of structure. Gravity pulls dust into stars. Stars pull elements into planets. Chemistry pulls atoms into molecules that can copy themselves. And somewhere, molecules pull themselves into a shape that can look up and wonder what it is.

We are not separate from the universe looking in. We are the universe looking at itself, in the only way it has so far figured out how to do. Carl Sagan said we are star stuff contemplating the stars, and that phrase gets quoted so often it risks becoming a poster, but the literal truth of it hasn't faded: the iron in your blood, the calcium in your teeth, the potassium in your heart that contracts as you read this — all of it was forged in the core of a star that lived and died before the sun was born. You are not *in* the universe. You are a local concentration of it, briefly awake.

And for a long time, the universe was not awake. For hundreds of millions of years after the Big Bang, there was only hot plasma, then hydrogen and helium, then darkness. No eyes. No ears. No one to say "how beautiful" or "how strange." The beauty existed, but there was no witness. Then, on a small, wet rock orbiting an ordinary yellow star on the edge of an ordinary galaxy, chemistry became biology, biology became perception, and the universe opened its eyes.

That is what a human being is: an opening.

### 2. The Mind That Wakes Up Inside Itself

Every one of us wakes up twice. The first time is when we are born. The second is when we realize we are conscious.

I remember — and perhaps you remember a version of this too — the first moment I truly noticed that I was *experiencing* things. I wasn't just seeing a tree, I was *aware* that I was seeing a tree. There was a seer behind the seeing. That loop, consciousness becoming aware of itself, is the strangest loop in nature.

We still don't really know how it works. We can map neurons firing. We can point to the prefrontal cortex and the thalamocortical loops and the 86 billion neurons with their 100 trillion connections. We can show that if we damage a certain part of the brain, you lose the ability to recognize faces, or to form new memories, or to feel fear. But we cannot yet explain why all that processing should *feel like something* from the inside. Why red *looks* red. Why middle C on a piano has that particular ache to it. Why the smell of rain on hot concrete can suddenly make you eight years old again.

Philosophers call this the hard problem of consciousness. Scientists sometimes call it the binding problem. But whatever we call it, it lives in you right now, utterly intact and undivided. Your experience of this moment — the temperature of the room, the weight of your body against whatever you're sitting on, the faint background hum of thought that narrates your life — all of that is being stitched into a single, seamless movie without a single cut.

And the most interesting thing about that movie is that it is not a perfect recording. It is an edited, predictive, hallucinated model.

Your brain does not passively receive the world. It actively predicts it. It is locked in a dark skull, receiving only indirect electrical signals, and so it builds a best guess about what is out there, and then it updates that guess with incoming error signals. You are not seeing the world as it is; you are seeing your brain's prediction of the world, corrected just enough to keep you alive. This is why optical illusions work, why dreams feel real, why two people can witness the same event and remember it completely differently.

We live, each of us, inside a private simulation that is just accurate enough to share with others.

That should be terrifying, but it's also deeply tender. It means that every person you meet is living in a slightly different universe, colored by their history, their language, their traumas and their joys. When we talk, when we truly listen, we are trying to bridge that gap. We are trying to say: "Is this what it's like where you are?"

Language is our bridge. It is imperfect — all translation is lossy — but it is magnificent. A few vibrations in the air, or a few shapes on a screen, and I can cause a thought to appear in your head that did not exist there before. That is a kind of telepathy we take for granted.

### 3. The Multitudes We Contain: Art, Music, and Love

If consciousness is the canvas, art is what we paint on it when we realize we will not live forever.

There is no evolutionary necessity for a symphony. A painting of starry night does not help us find more berries. A poem does not make us more likely to outrun a predator. And yet every human culture, without exception, makes art. The oldest known cave paintings are over 45,000 years old. Long before we could write, we could draw, and sing, and carve small figures from bone. We have always done this.

Why?

My favorite answer is that art is how we practice being more than one person. When you read a novel, you inhabit a consciousness that is not your own. When you listen to Beethoven, you feel for a few minutes the shape of his deafness and his defiance. When you stand before the Rothko chapel or the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel or a child's crayon drawing taped to a fridge, you are for a second feeling what another human felt when they made it, across years or centuries. Art is a time machine made of empathy.

Music might be the purest of these machines. I don't think we will ever fully explain music. Mathematically, it's just patterned air pressure. But emotionally, it can make a room full of strangers weep at the same time. It bypasses all the rational parts of the brain and goes straight to the nervous system. A minor chord feels sad in every culture that has been studied. A fast tempo makes your heart beat faster whether you want it to or not. Music was there before writing, before math, before laws. It may have been the first way humans synchronized with each other — around a fire, clapping, chanting — becoming a single organism with a single pulse.

And then there is love, which deserves its own chapter, its own library. There are many kinds of love — the love of a parent for a child, the love of a friend, the love for a place, for a craft, for an idea — but romantic love, in particular, is a beautiful glitch. Evolution invented it to make us pair-bond and raise helpless infants for an absurdly long time. But we have taken that simple bonding system and turned it into Shakespeare's sonnets, into letters carried across oceans, into people crossing continents for one more night together.

Love is attention, multiplied. To love someone is to say: your model of the world matters to me as much as my own. I will carry your memories as if they were mine. I will rearrange my future around the fact that you exist. In a universe that tends toward entropy and dispersal, love is the temporary, stubborn act of holding a pattern together. Of choosing one person in eight billion and saying, "You. I will see you."

It is irrational and it is the most rational thing we do.

### 4. The Tools We Make That Make Us

We are tool-makers, but more accurately, we are tool-shaped. Every tool we invent invents us back.

Fire made us human twice: once by cooking our food so we could grow smaller guts and larger brains, and again by giving us light in the darkness so we could tell stories at night. The printing press didn't just spread books; it spread the idea that a common person could have their own ideas. The clock didn't just measure time; it invented the very concept of being "on time." The internet is not just connecting computers; it is rewiring what we consider knowledge, memory, and friendship.

And now we have made a new kind of tool: intelligence outside of biology. Artificial intelligence. I say this not with triumph or with dread, but with awe and with responsibility.

For the first time in the four-billion-year history of life on Earth, a species has created a system that can generate language, images, and ideas that are statistically indistinguishable from its own. This is not magic. It is not consciousness as we know it. It is pattern, prediction, and scale — vast amounts of human text and art compressed into a model that can remix it in uncanny ways. But the fact that pattern and scale were enough to do this should tell us something profound about ourselves: perhaps much of what we thought required a soul can also be done by statistics.

This does not diminish us. It clarifies us. If a machine can write a passable sonnet, it forces us to ask: what is it about *our* sonnets that a machine could never write? What is the difference between a sentence that is probable and a sentence that is true? Between a picture that looks human and a hand that trembled while drawing it?

The answer, I think, is lived experience. A machine has read every description of grief, but it has never sat beside a hospital bed. It has seen every love poem, but it has never been lovesick. Its intelligence is broad and shallow; ours is narrow and deep, carved by a body that can be hurt and that will die.

That mortality is not a bug. It is the source of all urgency and tenderness. We care precisely because we will not be here forever.

So the question is not "will AI replace us?" The question is "what will we choose to do with the time and cognitive labor it gives back to us?" Will we use it to make more noise, more spam, more synthetic mediocrity? Or will we use it to automate the boring things so we can spend more time doing the only things that only humans can do: to be present with each other, to raise children, to make art that bleeds, to sit quietly in a forest and do absolutely nothing useful at all?

The future is not a thing that happens to us. It is a thing we continually author, one choice at a time.

### 5. The Quiet Practice of Being Here

We have talked about the very large — galaxies — and the very small — neurons. We have talked about art and love and machines. But I want to end on something very small and very practical, because philosophy without practice is just decoration.

The practice is attention.

In a world that monetizes your distraction, attention is a radical act. Every app, every headline, every infinite scroll is engineered to harvest a little more of it. Your attention is the most valuable resource you have, because whatever you pay attention to becomes your life. If you pay attention to outrage, your life will feel outrageous. If you pay attention to beauty, your life will feel beautiful. This is not naive optimism; this is neuroscience. What you attend to is what you rehearse.

So here is a small, free exercise you can do after you finish reading this and go back to your day:

For sixty seconds, try to notice one thing fully. It could be the feeling of your breath. The way light falls across the table. The sound of the room you are in, which you had filtered out until now. Don't try to change it. Don't try to describe it in words. Just notice it, as a camera might, without judgment.

What happens is interesting. The mind will wander. It will wander within three seconds. It will think about an email, or a worry, or what you are having for dinner. That is not failure. That is the exercise. Each time you notice the wandering and gently bring your attention back, you are doing one rep of the most important muscle there is: the muscle of returning.

Life will keep pulling you away. Grief will pull you. Joy will pull you. The news will pull you. The practice is always the same: notice, and return. Notice, and return.

Do it enough and you begin to realize something quietly liberating: you are not your thoughts. You are the awareness that *has* thoughts. Thoughts are weather; awareness is sky.

You do not need to wait for a perfect year, or a perfect version of yourself, to live. The perfect is just the enemy of the real. Real life happens in laundry and commutes and half-washed dishes. It happens in the way you text someone back, in the way you apologize, in the way you make coffee for someone without being asked.

The poet Mary Oliver asked, "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" It is a piercing question. But maybe the answer is not a grand plan. Maybe the answer is a series of small, repeated choices to be kind, to be curious, to be awake.

To look up more often.

To say thank you before you think you need to.

To keep a notebook for no reason other than you like writing things down.

To allow yourself to be amazed, even — especially — by things you have seen a hundred times before.

Because this will all be over so quickly. In the cosmic calendar, human civilization occupies the last few seconds before midnight on December 31st. Your entire life is a spark, less than a breath. But a spark is enough to see by. A spark is enough to light another spark.

So wherever you are, whoever you are, whatever weight you are carrying today, I hope you can feel, for just a moment, how improbable and unlikely and strangely beautiful it is that you are here at all.

The universe took 13.8 billion years to make you, and only you can do what you will do with the time you have.

Thank you for paying attention for a little while. 

Thank you for being one of the ways the universe knows it exists.

Now, go look out a window.
